notes.meaning: Paul explains that he must keep on boasting, even though doing so brings him no personal benefit. His opponents in Corinth had bragged about their spiritual experiences, so he turns to genuine visions and revelations that came straight from the Lord. A vision is something shown to the eyes, while a revelation is God uncovering hidden truth.

Paul speaks about himself in the third person to stay humble, describing a Christian man who was suddenly caught up to the third heaven fourteen years earlier. In common Jewish thought, the third heaven meant God's own dwelling place, far above the clouds and the stars. Paul could not tell whether his physical body went there or only his spirit, leaving the mystery entirely to God.

Paul repeats his statement to emphasize how real and mysterious this experience was. He knew this person intimately, yet he still could not explain how the journey took place. Only God knew whether it happened inside an earthly body or completely apart from it.

The man was caught up into Paradise, the place of joy and rest where God's presence dwells. While there, he heard holy words that human language is unable to describe and that no human being is permitted to repeat. These sacred truths were given to strengthen Paul privately, not to be published to the world.

Paul is willing to boast about that favored man who received heavenly glory, but when speaking of his ordinary life, he will boast only of his weaknesses. He separates that glorious experience from his own frail self so that he does not take credit for God's work. Boasting in human weakness makes sure that Christ gets all the honor.

If Paul chose to boast about his experiences, he would not be acting like a fool because he would be speaking the plain truth. However, he refuses to do so because he does not want anyone to think more highly of him than they should. He wants the church to judge him only by the life they see him live and the gospel message they hear him preach.

To stop Paul from becoming proud because of these extraordinary revelations, God allowed a painful thorn in the flesh to afflict him. Paul describes this hardship as a messenger of Satan sent to buffet and humble him. While the enemy meant it for harm, God used this deep trial to protect his servant from spiritual pride.

differ.view: Reformed teachers often view the thorn not as a single bodily illness, but as the whole sum of spiritual trials, persecutions, and inward temptations Paul struggled against.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Many Catholic interpreters historically understood the thorn as bodily temptation or lust, though other Catholic writers view it as a painful eye disease caused by Paul's blinding on the Damascus road.

notes.meaning: Paul took his deep distress straight to the Lord Jesus, begging three separate times for this torment to be removed. His repeated prayer echoes how Jesus himself prayed three times in Gethsemane before going to the cross. Believers can bring their deepest pains to the Lord again and again when seeking relief.

The Lord told Paul that his grace was all he needed, because divine power works best when human strength is completely gone. God did not remove the trial, but he promised the strength to carry it. Paul therefore decides to celebrate his weaknesses gladly so that the power of Christ can rest over him like a protective tent.

Because Christ is glorified through his struggles, Paul is fully content to face physical weaknesses, insults, hardships, and persecutions. None of these painful attacks can destroy him when they are endured for Jesus' sake. In the Christian life, feeling helpless in oneself opens the door to being truly strong in God.

Paul admits that talking so much about himself looks foolish, but the Corinthians forced him into it by giving ear to false leaders. The believers in Corinth should have spoken up to defend Paul instead of forcing him to defend his own ministry. Even though Paul views himself as nothing on his own, he was not one step behind those boastful super-apostles.

Paul had already displayed the genuine marks of an apostle while living and working among the Corinthians. He patiently endured suffering and opposition while God performed miraculous signs, wonders, and mighty deeds through him. These miracles were clear evidence that God had truly sent him.

differ.view: Many evangelicals believe that miraculous signs belonged uniquely to the original apostles to confirm their ministry, and that these special sign gifts ceased once the apostolic era ended.
Charismatic believers hold that miraculous signs were not limited to the apostles, but are spiritual gifts intended to continue throughout church history.

notes.meaning: Paul asks the Corinthians in what way their church was treated worse than other congregations he started. The only difference was that he refused to ask them for money to support him. He asks them with gentle sarcasm to forgive him for this wrong, showing how unreasonable their complaints were.

Paul is preparing to visit Corinth for a third time, and he assures them that he will still refuse to be a financial burden. He does not want their wealth; he wants their hearts and their spiritual good. Just as parents save up to provide for their children rather than demanding support from them, Paul acts as their spiritual father.

Paul is eager to spend all his resources and wear out his very life for the good of their souls. He cared far more about their spiritual health than about keeping his own comfort or energy. It broke his heart that the more love he poured out on them, the less love they seemed to return to him.

Paul repeats the slanderous rumors his opponents were spreading against him. These critics admitted that Paul never took money directly, but they claimed he was sly and used trickery to steal from them through others. They were accusing him of secretly taking money from the relief fund meant for the poor.

differ.view: Paul is rejecting a dishonest rumor made against him, so this verse must never be used to justify trickery or deceit in doing religious work.

notes.meaning: Paul refutes this rumor by directly appealing to the facts that the Corinthians already knew. He challenges them to name even one helper he sent who had ever cheated them or made money off them. His record of honesty was completely open for anyone to see.

Paul reminds them that he had sent Titus along with another trusted Christian brother to visit them. Titus never took advantage of them or asked for money, and the Corinthians knew it was true. Both Paul and Titus lived with the same clean motives and walked in the exact same path of financial honesty.

Paul corrects the idea that he is standing on trial before them like a guilty person making excuses. He speaks in the presence of God under the authority of Christ, who is his only judge. Everything he writes is done to build up their faith, not to win human approval.

Paul worries that when he arrives, he will find the church still torn apart by sinful behavior rather than walking in obedience. If they have not changed, they will not like how strict he will have to be in correcting them. He specifically fears sins that ruin fellowship, such as fighting, jealousy, bad tempers, selfish rivalries, gossip, pride, and chaos.

Paul is deeply concerned that his upcoming visit will bring him great sorrow and shame before God because of their rebellion. A faithful pastor feels heartbroken when church members stumble and refuse to turn away from sin. He fears having to mourn over believers who are still practicing pagan sexual sins without any repentance.
